messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Jason is twenty-one years old, married, and currently unemployed. He sits forward in the chair, his hands clasped tightly between his knees, and speaks in short, halting bursts. He is a tall, pale young man with close-cropped light brown hair, and he looks older than his age—not in his features, but in the hollowed, watchful quality of his eyes. He has come to therapy because his wife, Brianna, told him she could not keep living like this, and he could not argue with her.

The event that shattered everything happened eight months ago, in the parking lot of a gas station off Interstate 80. Jason was nineteen then, working nights at a warehouse, and his younger brother, Caleb, was seventeen. They had stopped for gas on the way home from a fishing trip. Jason was at the pump. Caleb was standing by the passenger door, stretching. A man walked up fast from behind the convenience store, and Jason saw him only in his peripheral vision—a sudden movement, a shape closing in. He turned. The man had a knife. He did not say a word. He stabbed Caleb twice in the chest and once in the stomach, then ran. Jason remembers the sound—a wet, percussive grunt from his brother—and the smell. There was a dumpster nearby, and the hot summer air was thick with the stench of rotting garbage and gasoline. That smell is still with him. Sometimes, when he is lying in bed at night, it fills his nose without warning, and he is back in that parking lot, frozen, watching his brother fall. Caleb survived, after three surgeries and a month in the ICU, but Jason has not survived the same way.

What Jason cannot do is put the event into words. When he tries to tell the story, even to Brianna, the sequence dissolves. He sees it in fragments—still images, like photographs laid out on a table. His brother’s hand reaching for the door handle. The blade. The blood on the asphalt. The man’s forearm, which is the body part he cannot stop seeing: a particular tattoo, a coiled snake, that he can summon in perfect visual detail even now. He cannot narrate the event because it does not live in language for him. It lives in pictures and smells and the sudden, overwhelming feeling that it is happening again—that he is standing at the pump, that the man is coming, that he will fail to move.

He has come to believe that his body has turned against him. His heart races when he walks into a quiet room. His palms sweat when a stranger walks too close. He tells the therapist that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger, even though he knows, logically, that he is safe. But knowing does not stop the reaction. He has also become convinced that he can no longer rely on himself. Before the attack, Jason was the steady one—the older brother, the one who worked double shifts, the one who fixed things. Now he cannot trust his own instincts. He froze at the gas station. He did not tackle the man, did not shield his brother. He stood there. And so he has come to believe that he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him: protecting the people he loves, keeping his head in a crisis, being someone worth counting on.

The avoidance began quietly and then consumed everything. He stopped watching television entirely, because any show with violence or suspense might show a knife, or a sudden attack, and he would be flooded with images he could not control. He stopped reading the news. He stopped scrolling social media. When his mother called to talk about Caleb’s recovery, he found himself unable to listen—her comments about the family, about how brave Caleb was being, about how they had all been through so much, felt like pressure on a bruise. He started leaving the room when she talked. More than anything, he cannot be alone. He cannot sit in a room by himself. The silence presses in, and the photographs in his mind start to move, and he feels the attack happening again in his chest. So he follows Brianna from room to room. He sleeps with the light on. He wakes at 2 a.m. and cannot fall back asleep, his mind replaying the smell of garbage and gasoline. Brianna works as a receptionist, and when she leaves for her shift, Jason drives to the public library and sits in the busiest corner, just to be near other people. He has stopped applying for jobs. He cannot imagine standing in a warehouse again, hearing footsteps behind him.

Two weeks ago, he hurt himself for the first time. He was home alone for forty minutes—Brianna had a dentist appointment—and the panic built until he could not breathe. He punched the wall, then took a shard of glass from a broken picture frame and cut his forearm. He says it released the pressure. He says it was the only thing that made the feeling stop. He told Brianna it was an accident, but she did not believe him.

Now he is here, in a therapist’s office, because he is terrified that he will lose his wife, and he is even more terrified that he will lose himself completely. He does not know how to stop the cycle. He does not know how to be alone. He does not know how to be the person he was before. But he came, and he is sitting in the chair, and that is the first thing he has done in months that feels like a choice.
